title: Google to Host Rival App Stores Inside Play Store Starting July 22
excerpt: After six years of litigation with Epic Games, Google will allow third-party app stores to access its full US app catalog through a new Play Catalog Access Program, marking the biggest change to Android app distribution since the Play Store launched.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • Starting July 22, third-party app stores will be available directly in the Google Play Store.
  • Google and Epic Games withdrew their settlement, enforcing an October 2024 court injunction for open competition.
  • Developers' apps will automatically appear in third-party stores unless they opt out, with Google processing downloads.
New Era for Android App Distribution
›Third-party app stores accessible via Google Play Store starting July 22, 2026.
›Developers' apps automatically listed in third-party stores unless opted out.
›Google's service fees apply to all downloads, regardless of store.
›Third-party stores face $5,000 onboarding and annual fees.
  • Starting July 22, third-party app stores will be downloadable directly from the Google Play Store in the US, with automatic access to Google's full catalog of apps and games.
  • Google and Epic Games jointly withdrew their proposed settlement, forcing Google to comply with the original October 2024 court injunction requiring open app store competition.
  • Developers' apps will automatically appear on participating third-party stores unless they opt out; downloads will still be processed through Google Play with its service fees applied.

End of a Six-Year Legal Battle

Google will begin hosting rival app stores inside the Google Play Store for US users starting July 22, 2026, marking the most significant change to Android app distribution in the platform's history.

The move follows a joint decision by Google and Epic Games to withdraw their previously proposed settlement in the long-running antitrust case, according to filings first reported by The Verge. With the settlement off the table, Google must now comply with the original October 2024 federal court injunction, which found that the company had unlawfully maintained monopoly power in Android app distribution and billing services.

"We've agreed with Epic to withdraw our motion to modify the US Court's injunction rather than prolonging this process which creates uncertainty for the ecosystem," Google spokesperson Dan Jackson told The Verge. "This allows us to focus on executing our recently announced global business model evolution to deliver greater app store choice, lower prices, and more opportunities for developers and users."

"Epic Games filed its antitrust lawsuit against Google in 2020, and a jury sided with Epic in 2024, finding that Google had maintained an illegal monopoly."

How the Play Catalog Access Program Works

Under the new system, Google has launched what it calls the Play Catalog Access Program. Third-party app stores that enroll in the program will be able to distribute apps directly from within the Google Play Store — a stark departure from the previous requirement that alternative stores be sideloaded by users, a process that most casual Android owners found cumbersome and avoided.

App and game listings that developers have submitted to Google Play will automatically be made available to participating third-party stores, unless developers explicitly opt out, according to Engadget. App downloads will still be completed through Google Play's infrastructure, and Google's service fees will continue to apply.

Third-party stores will face a $5,000 upfront fee for security review during onboarding and a $5,000 annual fee to maintain access to the Play catalog. They must also meet requirements including targeting users exclusively in the US — stores cannot use the Play catalog to distribute apps outside the United States.

From Settlement to Injunction

The path to this outcome was circuitous. Epic Games filed its antitrust lawsuit against Google in 2020, and a jury sided with Epic in 2024, finding that Google had maintained an illegal monopoly. US District Judge James Donato imposed an injunction requiring Google to open the Play Store to competing app stores.

Epic vs. Google: A Legal Timeline
2020
Epic Games files antitrust lawsuit against Google.
2024
Jury sides with Epic, ruling Google maintained illegal monopoly.
November 2025
Google and Epic propose a settlement, including an $800 million partnership.
2026
Settlement withdrawn; Google must comply with original court injunction.

Google and Epic reached a settlement in November 2025 that would have allowed a less sweeping "Registered App Stores" program — third-party stores that registered with Google would get a simplified sideloading flow but would still need to be installed outside the Play Store. The settlement also included an $800 million partnership between the companies, according to Android Authority.

Both parties ultimately concluded that court approval of the modified settlement was unlikely, and jointly withdrew it. The original, more aggressive injunction now stands.

Global Changes Too, but Different

The stores-within-a-store model applies only to the US market. Internationally, Google is moving ahead with its Registered App Stores program as part of its broader settlement with Epic. The company has also lowered its global commission structure: in-app purchase fees drop to 20%, and recurring subscription fees fall to 10%, according to GSMArena.

Separately, developers can now offer alternative payment options or link users to their own websites for purchases within their app listings — changes that apply in the UK, European Economic Area, and United States.

What It Means for Users and Developers

For Android users in the US, the practical impact is straightforward: starting next week, they will be able to browse and install third-party app stores without leaving the Play Store or navigating security warnings associated with sideloading. Epic Games is expected to be among the first to launch a store through the program.

For developers, the change is a double-edged sword. Their apps gain automatic exposure across new storefronts, potentially reaching users who prefer alternative marketplaces. But they also lose some control unless they actively opt out, and Google's fees remain in place regardless of which store facilitates the download.

The decision sets a precedent that will be closely watched in Europe, where the Digital Markets Act is pushing similar openness requirements, and in markets across Asia where Google's Play Store dominance faces growing regulatory scrutiny.
image_caption: A smartphone displaying mobile applications. Starting July 22, 2026, Google will allow third-party app stores to be downloaded directly from the Google Play Store in the United States.
nri_angle: The ruling could reshape how Indian-origin app developers distribute their products in the US market, and sets a precedent for similar regulatory moves in India and other markets where Google's Play Store dominance is under scrutiny.
